newsitem.title: UK: FX market yet to stake serious money on EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FX market yet to stake serious money on EMU delay.

text.p: The currency markets are buzzing with talk of delay to European economic and monetary union -- but players have yet to put serious money where their mouths are.
Analysts said the mark should remain robust, however, as the scale of the European Union's current turmoil over the key budget stability pact dawns on the market.

The mark jumped against its satellites on Monday when France said it needed time to study the pact -- igniting fears the whole EMU project would be postponed. But it failed to build on those gains and was ensconced in established ranges on Tuesday.

"We had a bit of a mini-wobble, but if the market seriously believed there was going to be a delay in EMU we wouldn't be seeing the markets as calm as they are," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

The mark hit highs of 3.3825 French francs and 84.78 pesetas after France dropped its bombshell on Monday, but was back at 3.3800/10 and 84.66/69 by midsession on Tuesday. It had ended here at 3.3763/66 and 84.57/59 last Friday.
The lira was less resilient, trading at 989.00/30 per mark on Tuesday versus Monday's low of 989.20 and Friday's close of 986.00/30, but was still well above its June 2 low of 995.30.
One reason for the relatively steady performance by the mark crosses is that market opinion is torn between two conflicting scenarios, analysts said.

The first scenario -- the one that propelled the mark higher on Monday -- is that EMU will be delayed beyond its scheduled start date on 1 January 1999. That traditionally boosts the German unit as the risk that it will be swallowed up into in a weaker single currency is perceived to recede.
The alternative is the timely launch of a broad, soft euro.
Fears of a weak euro were fuelled when the left wing -- which has made clear its desire to see a broad swathe of countries launch EMU -- swept to power in France on June 1.

A row between Bonn and the Bundesbank over plans to revalue assets, plus a jump in German unemployment, intensified those concerns as the market puzzled over just how Germany would cut its deficit to three percent of GDP as required for EMU.
France's request to go slow on the stability pact has set it up for a clash with Germany, which initiated the pact as a means of enforcing budgetary rigour in the EMU age, analysts said.
But the market is so far remaining sanguine.

"Given the political will to create the whole thing, people believe, and I think probably rightly, that they will weave a way between the two sides," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank of America here.
Market tension is sure to stay high for now, though, as nervous players trade on the latest headline or comment from EU official, analysts said.

And with a Franco-German summit looming on Friday ahead of an EU summit in Amsterdam next week -- and no guarantee that either of those will fully resolve the current conflict -- these edgy conditions could persist for some time.

"Since the stability pact represents the very essence of the philosophical differences between France and Germany over macro-economic policy it is difficult to envisage an easy painless fix," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Signs are, then, that the mark will remain sturdy on the European crosses as EMU-delay talk continues to circulate.

"The reaction on the crosses has been fairly muted but I think as the seriousness of the problem over the stability pact sinks in and the risk that has for the whole process, that will give the mark a firmer tone," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust in London.
"But it may be a slow grind rather than a huge leap higher."
